transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-27
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (AstraMed MLOps), Carlos Ruiz (AstraMed CTO), Elena Park (AstraMed Security)

Summary:
Short discovery for Private/VPC deployment. AstraMed is evaluating Redwood Private behind their VPC for HIPAA workloads. Main concerns: no public egress, BYOK/KMS, region/residency (need us-west-2 + eu-west-1), VPC peering vs PrivateLink, transit gateway, and audit logs. They want network requirements and an SE deep-dive and pilot.

Topics:
- VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, Transit Gateway
- Private endpoints, NAT/eS, egress control
- KMS/BYOK and HSM integration
- Region constraints and multi-region setup
- RBAC, audit logs, SOC2/HIPAA requirements
- Pilot/bench plan and next steps

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: All right good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Jordan from Redwood, AE on your account. With me is Priya, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Maya Chen: Hi Jordan, hey Priya — Maya here. Good, excited to dig in, we have a lot of questions on networking.
[00:18] Carlos Ruiz: Carlos — quick note, we're on a tight timeline, looking at a pilot in May if possible.
[00:23] Priya Rao: Awesome, thanks. Before we start, can you confirm this call is safe to discuss architecture? And Elena from security is on?
[00:30] Elena Park: Yep I'm here. We'll keep high level but want specifics on logging/encryption as we go.
[00:36] Jordan Lee: Great. The agenda: we'd like to understand your constraints, current infra, why Private vs Hosted/Dedicated, and then we can map Redwood's options — VPC peering, PrivateLink, transit, region mapping, and next steps. Sound good?
[00:46] Maya Chen: Yep. For context, AstraMed handles patient data, so HIPAA. We can't have model payloads going over the public internet. Also, we need BYOK, audit logs retained one year, and we prefer to own the VPC.
[00:59] Jordan Lee: Understood. Quick qual: what cloud provider(s) are you using? Primary region?
[01:05] Carlos Ruiz: We're 80% on AWS — us-west-2 primary, second region eu-west-1. We also have a GCP project for analytics but core MLOps is AWS.
[01:14] Priya Rao: Good. So Redwood Private can deploy into your VPC — we support both VPC peering and AWS PrivateLink endpoints. For HIPAA we usually recommend PrivateLink or Transit Gateway depending on scale, because peering has some limitations with cross-account routing and if you need many VPCs TGW is cleaner.
[01:32] Elena Park: Can you explain the difference operationally? We want minimal attack surface.
[01:36] Priya Rao: Sure. VPC peering is a direct route between two VPCs — simpler, but it's point-to-point. PrivateLink (AWS PrivateLink) exposes an interface endpoint in your VPC that speaks to Redwood's service endpoint in our account — it is a managed ENI with private IPs and doesn't require route table propagation across many VPCs. Transit Gateway is for hubs, good if you need connectivity across many VPCs or accounts. PrivateLink typically gives you better isolation — inbound traffic stays within AWS, no internet, and you can apply SGs to the ENIs.
[02:05] Maya Chen: Do we get egress control? We don't want the service to call out to the internet, e.g., model downloads or telemetry.
[02:12] Jordan Lee: Yes. For Redwood Private we can run in your VPC without public egress. Model artifacts can be preloaded into the deployment or pulled from your S3 via VPC endpoints and restricted to private endpoints. Telemetry is configurable — we can either route logs to your Kinesis/S3 or push to our control plane over a private link.
[02:29] Carlos Ruiz: Hmm pushing to your control plane... we'd prefer control plane traffic go over PrivateLink as well, or maintain a pull model. What options do we have?
[02:36] Priya Rao: We support a private control plane option where the control plane API is reachable via PrivateLink into your account. Alternatively, you can run private control plane components in your VPC in air-gapped setups. For most customers the PrivateLink model is sufficient — all control plane APIs are bound to private endpoints and mutual TLS is enforced.
[02:53] Elena Park: BYOK for KMS — do you integrate with our KMS or do we hand off keys? We need HSM or dedicated keys.
[03:00] Jordan Lee: You keep the keys. Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS keys for data at rest. For encryption-in-use we integrate with HSM-backed KMS if needed. We'll need an IAM role/trust to allow Redwood's instances to use your key for disk encryption or we can bring pre-encrypted AMIs. We'll detail options in the network/security doc.
[03:18] Maya Chen: What's the network footprint — CIDR ranges, ports, SGs? We need to pre-approve in our security policy.
[03:24] Priya Rao: Typical footprint: a small set of private IP ranges for the Redwood nodes — we'll provide a recommended /27 or /26 depending on scale. Ports: we require outbound to your S3 endpoints for model fetch if you choose remote fetching, and inbound on the PrivateLink interface — we'll provide the security group templates. We'll include terraform and CloudFormation examples.
[03:43] Jordan Lee: Also note we can support per-tenant isolation with dedicated subnets and security groups; for larger customers we deploy dedicated node pools per team.
[03:50] Carlos Ruiz: About regions — we need at least us-west-2 and eu-west-1 with data residency. Can Redwood run control plane in one region and compute in another?
[03:59] Priya Rao: Compute must be in the region you specify (we deploy the serving runtime into your VPC in that region). Control plane communication can be regionalized via PrivateLink endpoints in each region, or we can set up a regional control plane in eu-west-1 for EU workloads if you need strict residency.
[04:14] Elena Park: Latency concerns — if control plane cross-region, will that affect token-level latency or just control ops?
[04:19] Priya Rao: Control plane traffic is primarily orchestration — start/stop, health checks. Inference traffic (token path) stays inside your VPC and will be local to the compute nodes. So inference latency is determined by the compute region and your clients.
[04:30] Maya Chen: Are there any managed NAT or internet egress we should watch? We don't want accidental egress to pull model updates directly from public repos.
[04:36] Jordan Lee: We avoid public egress by default for Private. If you want model updates, we can either have you place model artifacts in an S3 bucket with an S3 gateway endpoint, or we can run a private model registry inside your network. We'll include a recommended IAM/cross-account role pattern.
[04:51] Carlos Ruiz: How about autoscaling — does it create new ENIs or subnets dynamically? Our security folks need to know for IP allowlist.
[04:58] Priya Rao: It will scale within the allocated subnets; new instances get private IPs from the subnet pool so you should set aside headroom in the CIDR. We can also provide predictable IP ranges by preallocating /27 blocks for scaling.
[05:12] Elena Park: Audit logs: we need immutable logs for a year and log shipping to our Splunk/S3. Can Redwood push logs to our endpoints?
[05:20] Jordan Lee: Yes. We can export audit logs to your S3 or push into your logging endpoint over a private connection. We support structured logs with request ids and token counts. Retention is configurable; we'll include the default retention and how to set up long-term archiving.
[05:33] Maya Chen: What's the setup time? If we want a pilot in May, is it realistic?
[05:38] Priya Rao: For a pilot with basic VPC PrivateLink and a small node pool, we usually see 1-2 weeks once networking is in place. If you need BYOK/KMS and SOC checks, add an extra week for security approvals. Given your timeline, if you can provide CIDRs and approve PrivateLink we'll aim for early May pilot.
[05:54] Carlos Ruiz: Pricing question — is Private billed as a flat infra fee or usage?
[05:58] Jordan Lee: Typically Private is a mix: base platform fee plus reserved capacity pricing for GPUs, or pay-as-you-go for burst. We'll send a pricing sheet — for pilot we can do a short-term eval pricing.
[06:10] Maya Chen: One of our engineers asked about KV cache and batching — sorry, that's internal but we want to understand memory footprints because of instance sizing.
[06:18] Priya Rao: No problem. The runtime uses KV cache per-session; memory scales with sequence length. For heavy chat loads we size instances for larger host memory. We'll include recommended instance types and quantization options in the doc.
[06:31] Jordan Lee: Quick check — do you foresee connecting multiple AWS accounts to the Redwood Private deployment?
[06:36] Carlos Ruiz: Yes, our dev, staging, prod are separate accounts. Ideally we'd like cross-account access.
[06:41] Priya Rao: OK for multi-account: PrivateLink in a central account or Transit Gateway are common. We can also set up endpoint services in each account. We'll map recommended patterns in the doc based on number of accounts.
[06:53] Elena Park: Service accounts and IAM — how granular is RBAC? We want to control who can spin up models and who can access logs.
[06:59] Jordan Lee: Redwood integrates with your identity provider for SAML/SSO and we support fine-grained RBAC for routes and model deployments. We'll include examples for least privilege roles.
[07:10] Maya Chen: Anything we should be mindful of regarding our CNI or EKS setup? We're on EKS Fargate for some services and managed nodegroups for others.
[07:19] Priya Rao: We can interface with both. For EKS-hosted components we recommend using dedicated subnets and security groups; when running on EC2 nodepools we control kernel settings for high-performance inference. If you need Fargate compatibility we'll call that out — latency and GPU availability differ.
[07:33] Carlos Ruiz: Does Redwood require any host-level agents or do you run everything as containers in our VPC?
[07:39] Priya Rao: We deploy containerized runtime images into your VPC. No persistent host agents. For monitoring we'll ship sidecar exporters that push metrics to your Prometheus or pushgateway over private endpoints.
[07:49] Elena Park: Data residency again — if we process EU data in eu-west-1, we want keys in region and logs stay in region. Is that supported?
[07:56] Priya Rao: Yes, we can regionally scope both compute and key management. We'll recommend separate deployments per region for strict residency.
[08:06] Maya Chen: Any gotchas with Azure or GCP if we later expand?
[08:10] Priya Rao: We have private endpoint patterns for Azure (Private Link/ExpressRoute) and GCP (VPC Peering/Interconnect/Private Service Connect). We can share those templates if you plan multi-cloud.
[08:21] Jordan Lee: I'll note to include Azure/GCP patterns in the follow-up doc.
[08:25] Carlos Ruiz: Security: agentless or do you need any inbound SSH? Our policy forbids inbound SSH.
[08:31] Priya Rao: No inbound SSH required. All maintenance is done via our orchestration over PrivateLink or out-of-band maintenance windows coordinated with you.
[08:40] Elena Park: What about OS/patching visibility? We need SBOM and patch cadence for images.
[08:45] Jordan Lee: We provide SBOMs for our images and a monthly patch schedule; hotfixes for critical vulnerabilities are pushed quicker. We'll include certs and SBOMs in the compliance pack.
[08:56] Maya Chen: Ok good. On the encryption side — do you support mTLS for service-to-service?
[09:00] Priya Rao: Yes, we support mutual TLS on control plane and can enable mTLS between internal services if desired. For PrivateLink the interface endpoints can require TLS; we also apply token auth.
[09:12] Carlos Ruiz: How do we do failover between regions? If us-west-2 goes down, can eu-west-1 serve latency-sensitive requests?
[09:19] Priya Rao: For active-active you can deploy compute in both regions and use global routing at your app layer. We also support automatic fallback to a lower-capacity model variant in another region, but cross-region inference will increase latency — so recommended pattern is regional compute for low latency.
[09:36] Maya Chen: Anything else from Redwood that typically trips up customers during onboarding?
[09:40] Priya Rao: Common items: not reserving enough CIDR space for scaling, delays in IAM cross-account role approvals, and key usage policies blocking our service role. We'll send a checklist to help avoid those issues.
[09:52] Jordan Lee: Great. Quick recap and next steps: Jordan sends Private network requirements doc, Priya schedules SE deep-dive and pilot bench plan, AstraMed to provide network CIDRs and compliance items. Anything else?
[10:05] Maya Chen: Please include the sample terraform and CloudFormation snippets, and a sample S3 policy for restricted model artifacts.
[10:12] Jordan Lee: Yes. Also sending SOC2 and HIPAA attestation docs.
[10:16] Carlos Ruiz: We'll aim to have the network diagram by Friday.
[10:20] Elena Park: I'll review the compliance pack and get back with any showstoppers.
[10:24] Jordan Lee: Perfect, thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the doc and a calendar invite for the SE deep-dive.
[10:30] Maya Chen: Thanks, talk soon.

End of call.

Notes on transcription: occasional mislabels and filler; some technical terms may be slightly transcribed (e.g., "PrivateLink" sometimes spelled "private link", "KV cache" transcribed as "K-V cache").
